prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and for its development to fractional uncertainties of 10^-18, opening a new regime of precision measurement.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B017 to B015, alone. This is a judgment on the record and not a response to the count of supporters. The question I put to myself is the one I always put: can we be absolutely sure that we have found the people who did the original work, and is the result experimentally verified? For the lattice clock the answer is clearer than for any other entry. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength condition and demonstrated the lattice, which is an original idea with a named originator, and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 regime with the systematics understood. Independent clock-to-clock comparisons at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE are the experimental verification, and they are stronger than what B017 can show today. As to what is new relative to 2005 and 2012, I can say it in one sentence: the comb made optical frequencies countable and the ion work showed control of a single quantum system, whereas the lattice clock showed that thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once with the leading light shifts cancelled, which is a different principle and not the same clock made better. It is also a new tool that opens a door, to millimetre-scale redshift measurements, constancy-of-constants tests and dark-matter searches, which is the kind of invention that I weigh heavily. My round-1 preference for B017 rested on the strength of the phenomenon, and I still think that field is a future candidate, but after the exchange I cannot say I am sure of the credit or the maturity there.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B015 is still lineage and degree: a critic can say that it is a very large quantitative step on the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I accept that risk and think the citation must name the invention, the magic-wavelength lattice, and not just the precision. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I would leave it out of the citation; it is timing and not evidence. The two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and I cannot weigh those contributions from memory. I would welcome an expert report before the final ballot, but nobody has proposed a different pair. For B017, my own case against, which I retain, is the unresolved credit for Cao and for the Dean, Young, Efetov and Yacoby groups, and the unsettled mechanism. Those are the reasons I give up B017 as first choice and do not simply defend it.

responses.point: Bernhard prefers B015 over B017 because we would not want to prize something before we know why it works, and he asks whether the opening strength of B015 reflects merit or only safe consensus.
responses.response: I take both halves of this seriously. On B017 I agree that the pairing mechanism is open, and that was the point on which my own certainty weakened most. On the suspicion of a safe consensus, I tested it by asking what I would need to see for the clock if it were not already popular, and the answer holds: there is a named inventor, a distinct principle, and agreement among several independent laboratories at 10^-18. That is a stronger test than a number of first-place votes. I therefore move toward B015 but for the reasons of attribution and verification, not for the sake of the majority.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth asks how a precision-metrology prize is weighed against a discovery and asks whether the redefinition of the second should be awaited. She and Stefan were asked by the chair to draft the citation wording.
responses.response: I would accept the redefinition as timing only and leave it out of the citation, since the demonstrated 10^-18 agreement stands on its own and waiting a year buys no new evidence about who did the original work. I would ask that the draft say what Katori invented, the lattice interrogated at the magic wavelength, so the citation does not read as a prize for a better number. I would also ask you whether the Lemonde and Pfau lattice-adjacent proposals are precursors or contemporaneous, since that bears on whether Katori is the right originator. I could not settle that from memory.

responses.point: Stefan names lineage as the strongest objection, the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and the case that rests on a step of two orders of magnitude plus a new scheme. He also records his Boulder connection to the Hall tradition.
responses.response: I agree with your framing: the case rests on the new scheme and not the size of the step alone, and that is why I now support B015, having ranked it as an alternative in round 1. Your disclosure is helpful and I think it should be noted in the record, though I do not see it as a bar given that you have no collaboration with the credited pair. I would add that the reproduction at several laboratories is what turns the Katori idea from a proposal into a verified invention, and I would want the final citation to say that the scheme was demonstrated.

responses.point: Olle holds B051 as first choice, and agrees that his weak point is the credit, with Mele omitted and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and the Fu-Kane work outside the trio. He also said B017 is less mature than a field whose interpretation is settled.
responses.response: Your point on maturity of B017 is one I now accept, and you are right that B051 is the more settled field. But the credit problem you name is the one that keeps me from joining you: a Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan trio leaves out Mele, and Mele is a co-originator, so I cannot be absolutely sure that we have identified the original people. If the committee could find a defensible way to credit the Kane-Mele pair together with Molenkamp I would look again, but the three-person limit appears to make that a different trio from the one you propose. Until then B051 stays an alternative for me.

responses.point: Ulf proposes a two-part prize that pairs B015 with B040 (Halzen alone), and concedes that the single-name IceCube credit is the weak point.
responses.response: I cannot support the second part. A sole credit for a collaboration of this size, with AMANDA and Baikal in the history and the source identifications still developing, is something I could not say is the original work of one person, and no historical record has been produced in round 1 that would change that. Your own concession on the weak point seems to me decisive. I would rather the committee give a single clean prize than a two-part one in which the second part cannot be defended, and the three-person limit gives no room for a better B040 credit.

responses.point: The chair asks whether, if B015 stands alone, the committee wants a second part at all, and which candidate would be distinct and fit the three-person limit.
responses.response: My answer is no: none of the other candidates fits. B015 uses two names, which leaves a single name, and the only entry with a single credited name is B040, which I have just said I cannot defend. Every other entry needs three or more names. I would also say, as a member who has chaired this committee, that a single-part prize is an entirely proper outcome and need not be filled out.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are the right pair given Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, which I cannot judge from memory and for which I would want an expert report.
Whether the lattice clock is distinct enough in principle from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or whether it is mainly a very large quantitative step; I judge it distinct, but this is a matter of judgment.
Whether the credit and mechanism questions in B017 will be resolved in the coming years, in which case I would expect to support it later.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should lead the committee to wait; I treat it as timing and not evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or any other credited name. I have no collaboration with the lattice-clock community; my work is in transmission electron microscopy of materials and interfaces. Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics, which is an institutional connection that is not tied to any candidate I now prefer. I note Stefan Kroll's disclosure of a scientific lineage to Boulder, and Goran Johansson's closeness to B012, and neither bears on my position.
